props.title: The Safety of Objects

sections.content: **The Safety of Objects** (2001) represents a pivotal moment in independent suburban drama, following the interconnected lives of four families dealing with trauma and isolation. Director Rose Troche adapts A.M. Homes' short stories into a precursor of the multi-narrative style that would later define films like **Crash** (2004) and **Little Children** (2006). Glenn Close delivers a haunting performance as a mother caring for her comatose son while forming an unusual attachment to her neighbor's doll, showcasing the kind of complex suburban darkness that **American Beauty** (1999) brought to mainstream attention.

sections.content: The film's release coincided with a wave of suburban critique cinema that emerged in the late 1990s and early 2000s. While **Pleasantville** (1998) used fantasy to deconstruct suburban ideals and **Revolutionary Road** (2008) examined its 1950s foundations, **The Safety of Objects** takes a more contemporary approach, showing how modern families cope with isolation despite physical proximity. Patricia Clarkson's performance as a divorced mother navigating both professional ambition and family obligations echoes similar themes in **Laurel Canyon** (2002). SUBHEAD: Suburban Alienation and Material Culture

The film's treatment of material possessions as emotional surrogates creates a direct through-line to later works like **The Virgin Suicides** (1999) and **White Noise** (2022). Director Troche uses objects - particularly the notorious doll - as metaphors for the ways people process grief and maintain control. This technique would later be refined in films like **The Lovely Bones** (2009), where personal artifacts become totems of memory and loss. Joshua Jackson's character's relationship with his sister's possessions particularly resonates with similar themes in **Things We Lost in the Fire** (2007).
